summary: Ustaz Azlan opens with the trials that struck his friends, then turns to episode 32: Quraysh's boycott of Bani Hashim and Bani Abdul Muttalib after the shock of Hamzah and Umar accepting Islam. Abu Talib gathered the wider family in Shi'b Abi Talib while Quraysh declared a total economic and social blockade, hung in the Kaaba. For about three years they lived on high alert, in hunger and psychological strain, which the ustaz compares with Gaza. He tells of the help of Hakim ibn Hizam and Khadijah, the campaign of five non-Muslims led by Hisham ibn Amr to cancel the pact, the revelation that termites had eaten the document except Allah's name, and the end of the boycott. He links present-day lessons to collective effort, including the New York mayoral election, and to history repeating as in the stories of the prophets.
keyPoints: The conversion of Hamzah and Umar alarmed the Quraysh elite, who openly resolved to kill the Prophet SAW and declared a boycott of Bani Hashim and Bani Abdul Muttalib.
Abu Talib gathered the wider family in Shi'b Abi Talib; some were not Muslim but stayed out of clan solidarity and principles of justice.
The pact cut off trade, marriage and movement entirely, and was hung inside the Kaaba.
For about three years they kept watch in shifts and went hungry, eating hide, twigs and leaves, while Abu Jahal blocked aid.
Hakim ibn Hizam and Khadijah sent supplies; Khadijah spent her wealth to support everyone besieged.
Five people from different clans, led by Hisham ibn Amr, planned and stood up together against the pact.
The Prophet SAW received revelation that termites ate the pact except Allah's name; Abu Talib challenged Quraysh and the pact was cancelled.
The ustaz urges us to see history repeat and to start good change by one person inviting another.

chapters.summary: Gratitude and the stories of friends tested by accidents.

chapters.title: Quraysh's reaction and the decision to kill the Prophet SAW
chapters.summary: After Hamzah and Umar became Muslim, the elite panicked and openly resolved to kill the Prophet SAW.

chapters.title: Abu Talib gathers the family
chapters.summary: Bani Hashim and Bani Abdul Muttalib, Muslim and not, united to protect the Prophet SAW.

chapters.title: Two aims of the boycott
chapters.summary: To split the families and to scare people off Islam through economic pressure.

chapters.title: Terms of the boycott pact
chapters.summary: No trade, no marriage, no free movement, with the document hung in the Kaaba.

chapters.title: High alert in Shi'b Abi Talib
chapters.summary: Watching in shifts, changing tents, and three years of emotional strain.

chapters.title: Comparison with Gaza and Palestinian leaders
chapters.summary: The ustaz compares the siege and assassination of Palestinian leaders with the suffering in the Shi'b.

chapters.title: Hunger and the reports of food
chapters.summary: Abu Jahal raised prices; reports of Sa'd and Bilal eating hide, twigs and leaves.

chapters.title: Hakim ibn Hizam and Khadijah
chapters.summary: Hakim sent camels of food; Abu Jahal blocked him and Khadijah spent her wealth.

chapters.title: Hisham ibn Amr and the five
chapters.summary: Hisham persuaded Zuhair, Mut'im, Abul Bukhtari and Zam'ah until the five planned together.

chapters.title: Standing up to cancel the pact
chapters.summary: The five stood one by one at the Kaaba against Abu Jahal.

chapters.title: Revelation: termites ate the pact
chapters.summary: The Prophet SAW told Abu Talib that termites ate the pact except Allah's name.

chapters.title: The boycott ends
chapters.summary: Abu Talib challenged Quraysh; the document was opened, found eaten, and people were led out.

chapters.title: A present-day example: the New York election

chapters.title: History repeats
chapters.summary: Allah told the stories of earlier prophets to steady the Prophet's heart; the pattern of Pharaoh repeats.

chapters.title: Q&A: da'wah during the boycott
chapters.summary: Da'wah was limited during the boycott, yet many embraced Islam afterwards after seeing their steadfastness.

lessons.title: Others' trials bring reflection
lessons.body: Seeing friends tested shows how comfortable we are.

lessons.title: Solidarity across faiths
lessons.body: Non-Muslims also stayed out of clan ties and principles of justice.

lessons.title: Suffering is often erased from history
lessons.body: This harshest stretch is little told, so we must keep the memory.

lessons.title: The Prophet's burden of feeling
lessons.body: The Prophet SAW bore seeing people suffer because they defended him.

lessons.title: Do good even before you are Muslim
lessons.body: Hakim ibn Hizam sent food though not yet Muslim and under threat.

lessons.title: Dare to be the first
lessons.body: Change begins with one stubborn person who finds a way and persuades others.

lessons.title: Strategy, not just emotion
lessons.body: Hisham built arguments and a coalition rather than just raging at Abu Jahal.

lessons.title: Human effort and Allah's help
lessons.body: Effort must be made, and Allah's help comes within the process even if unseen.

lessons.title: The Prophet's honesty was trusted
lessons.body: Abu Talib acted because the Prophet SAW never lied.

lessons.title: The Quran is relevant until the Last Day
lessons.body: The stories of earlier prophets steady hearts, and patterns repeat.

lessons.title: The truthful do not lose
lessons.body: If they die they are martyrs; if they win, they win.

lessons.title: One person inviting one person
lessons.body: Big change starts with small steps.

lessons.title: The danger of too much comfort
lessons.body: Without pressure, we forget the big picture and quarrel over small things.

glossary.meaning: Total economic and social blockade of Bani Hashim and Bani Abdul Muttalib.
The valley owned by Abu Talib behind the residential area, hemmed in by mountains.
The clan descended from Hashim; with Bani Abdul Muttalib, the Prophet's closest family.
A traitor who works with the enemy.
The season when killing is forbidden, so the Prophet SAW could go out to people.
A technique Hisham used to stir guilt by contrasting Zuhair's comfort with his relatives' hunger.
The insect that ate the pact except Allah's name.
Abu Jahal's nickname in Makkah because of his cleverness.

dalil.context: One report about food when supplies were cut off.
dalil.translation: Sa'd went out at night and heard his urine fall on something hard; it was animal hide. He washed it, burned it and crushed it into powder, drank it with water, and it was his food for three days.

dalil.context: A picture of the hunger in Shi'b Abi Talib.
dalil.translation: Bilal ibn Rabah said they ate twigs and leaves for lack of food, so their droppings were like a goat's.

dalil.context: When the pact proved eaten by termites, Abu Jahal called it magic; the ustaz cites Al-Qamar verse 2.
dalil.translation: Whenever the disbelievers see a sign, they turn away and say, ‘Same old sorcery!’
